subject: astronomy
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Which two planets are classed as inferior planets?
options: Mercury and Venus
Mars and Jupiter
Venus and Mars
Jupiter and Saturn
questions.explain: Inferior planets orbit the Sun inside Earth's orbit, and only Mercury and Venus do so.

questions.q: At which configuration is a superior planet best placed for observation?
options: Opposition
Superior conjunction
Inferior conjunction
Greatest elongation
questions.explain: At opposition a superior planet lies opposite the Sun in the sky, closest to Earth and fully illuminated, so it is brightest and visible all night.

questions.q: Why can Venus only be seen shortly after sunset or before sunrise?
options: As an inferior planet it never appears far from the Sun in the sky
It only shines when the Sun is below the horizon
Its orbit lies outside Earth's, keeping it near the horizon
It is too faint to see against a fully dark sky
questions.explain: Because Venus orbits inside Earth's orbit, its angular distance from the Sun is limited, so it is only visible near sunrise or sunset.

questions.q: What is the name given to the angle between a planet and the Sun as seen from Earth?
options: Elongation
Opposition
Parallax
Declination
questions.explain: Elongation is the angular separation between a planet and the Sun as viewed from Earth.

questions.q: Which planets show a full cycle of phases similar to the Moon?
options: The inferior planets, Mercury and Venus
The superior planets, such as Mars and Jupiter
All planets equally
Only Mars
questions.explain: Because Mercury and Venus orbit between Earth and the Sun, we see their sunlit side change through a complete set of phases.

questions.q: An observer records that a planet is never seen more than about 28 degrees from the Sun. Which planet is it?
options: Mercury
Venus
Mars
Jupiter
questions.explain: Mercury's small orbit gives it the smallest maximum elongation of about 28 degrees, keeping it very close to the Sun in the sky.

questions.q: Why does a superior planet appear brightest at opposition?
options: It is at its closest to Earth and fully illuminated by the Sun
It emits more of its own light at opposition
It is directly between the Earth and the Sun
It is at its furthest point from the Sun
questions.explain: At opposition the planet is nearest Earth and we see its fully lit face, so it appears at its brightest.

questions.q: During retrograde motion, how does a planet appear to move against the background stars?
options: Westward (east to west), opposite its usual motion
Eastward (west to east), its usual direction
Straight towards the celestial pole
It appears to stop and never moves again
questions.explain: Retrograde motion is the temporary apparent reversal in which a planet drifts westward against the stars, opposite to its normal prograde (eastward) motion.

questions.q: Why does a superior planet appear to undergo retrograde motion?
options: Earth, on its faster inner orbit, overtakes the slower-moving planet
The planet genuinely reverses the direction of its orbit
The Sun's gravity pulls the planet backwards
The planet slows down and falls behind the stars
questions.explain: As Earth catches up and passes a superior planet near opposition, the change in our line of sight makes the planet appear to move backwards.

questions.q: Over several weeks Mars is seen to drift westward against the stars before resuming its eastward motion. Near which configuration is this most likely occurring?
options: Opposition
Superior conjunction
Greatest elongation
Inferior conjunction
questions.explain: Retrograde motion of a superior planet occurs around opposition, when Earth overtakes it on the inside track.

questions.q: How did the Ptolemaic (geocentric) model account for retrograde motion?
options: Planets moved on small circles called epicycles
The Earth spun rapidly on its axis
The Sun pushed the planets back periodically
Planets orbited in perfect ellipses
questions.explain: In the geocentric model, planets were said to move on epicycles (small circles) whose combined motion produced apparent loops.

questions.q: In which direction do planets normally move against the background stars (prograde motion)?
options: West to east
East to west
North to south
South to north
questions.explain: Normal prograde motion is an eastward (west-to-east) drift of a planet against the stars from night to night.

questions.q: A student plots a superior planet's position over many nights and finds it traces a backwards loop or S-shape among the stars. What does this loop represent?
options: A period of retrograde motion as Earth overtakes the planet
The planet passing behind the Sun
The planet moving into inferior conjunction
A change in the planet's real orbital direction
questions.explain: The looping path is the apparent retrograde motion produced by Earth passing the planet near opposition.

questions.q: What causes aurorae in Earth's atmosphere?
options: Charged particles from the Sun striking atmospheric gases
Sunlight reflecting off high-altitude ice clouds
Meteoroids burning up in the upper atmosphere
Lightning in the upper atmosphere
questions.explain: Aurorae form when charged particles from the Sun (the solar wind) collide with and excite gas atoms in Earth's upper atmosphere, which then emit light.

questions.q: Why are aurorae usually seen at high latitudes near the poles?
options: Earth's magnetic field channels charged particles towards the magnetic poles
The atmosphere is only thick enough to glow near the poles
The Sun's light only reaches the polar regions
Sunspots are always directly above the poles
questions.explain: Earth's magnetic field guides incoming charged particles towards the polar regions, so aurorae are concentrated at high latitudes.

questions.q: What is the name given to the aurora seen in the southern hemisphere?
options: Aurora Australis
Aurora Borealis
Aurora Polaris
Aurora Meridianis
questions.explain: The southern lights are called the Aurora Australis, while the northern lights are the Aurora Borealis.

questions.q: Auroral activity tends to be strongest when the Sun is most active. Which of these is linked to increased aurorae?
options: Periods of high solar activity such as solar maximum
The Sun being at its faintest
A total lunar eclipse
Earth being furthest from the Sun
questions.explain: More frequent and intense aurorae occur around solar maximum, when increased solar activity sends more charged particles towards Earth.

questions.q: What causes an annual meteor shower?
options: Earth passing through the debris trail left by a comet
Fragments breaking off a nearby planet
Charged particles from the Sun entering the atmosphere
Dust rising from Earth's own surface
questions.explain: Meteor showers occur when Earth moves through the stream of dust and debris left along a comet's orbit, and this material burns up in the atmosphere.

questions.q: During a meteor shower, what is meant by the 'radiant'?
options: The point in the sky from which the meteors appear to spread out
The brightest meteor of the shower
The comet that produced the debris
The height at which meteors burn up
questions.explain: The radiant is the point, usually within a named constellation, from which the meteors of a shower appear to radiate due to perspective.

questions.q: An observer wants to watch the Perseid meteor shower, whose radiant lies in the constellation Perseus. At roughly what time of year should they observe?
options: August
January
April
June
questions.explain: The Perseids peak in mid-August, when Earth passes through the debris of comet Swift-Tuttle.
